Amid years of change, Derek Houston remains a constant for Sac State football

After entering the transfer portal following an injury-shortened season, the Rocklin native returns to the center of a rebuilt Hornet defense.
Jack Dann, Managing Editor • August 25, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:15
Instaread
Junior linebacker Derek Houston is interviewed during the program’s spring game Saturday, April 25, 2026. Houston is poised for a strong season after injuries derailed his sophomore year. (Photo by AJ Tinkess)

Sacramento State football has been a revolving door over the last four years, cycling through coaches, players and conferences since the departure of former head coach Troy Taylor.

Junior linebacker Derek Houston has watched the environment change from his place in the heart of the Hornet defense.

“I get this question a lot, everyone asks, ‘What’s it like moving like a different coach every year?’” Houston said. “I’m on my fifth position coach since I committed, so this is all just natural to me.”

Under Brennan Marion, who led the Hornets to a 7-5 record, Houston’s breakout sophomore year was cut short by injury. He logged 20 tackles in his first three games, including 11 stops and two sacks.

Days after the final game, Houston entered the transfer portal.

“I thought there was no chance of me coming back to Sacramento,” Houston said. “I wanted to stay here all my five years, but I had a sour taste in my mouth after last season.”

Like Houston, Marion departed in the offseason, but Sac State’s new coach had other plans for the junior linebacker.

“I talked to Coach [Alonzo] Carter, and he reaffirmed to me that he wanted to bring back the old Sac State, like the one that I joined initially under Coach Taylor and Coach [Andy] Thompson,” Houston said. “That automatically got me hooked.”

With Carter as their new playcaller, the Hornets spent the offseason rebuilding a transfer portal-gutted roster. More than 80 players from California joined the roster, several of whom, like Houston, hail from the greater Sacramento area.

The approach mirrors the Big Sky-winning teams Houston originally committed to, rosters constructed almost entirely from California talent.

Houston saw limited action in his first two seasons with Sac State before taking on a larger role in 2024. He started the year primarily on special teams before earning a starting role at linebacker by the end of the season.

“He’s a huge part of this defense,” senior defensive lineman Xavier Williams said. “He ties everything together.”

As Houston’s role on the field grew, so did his importance within the program. Carter sees him as the kind of dependable presence he wants to build his defense around.

“His leadership, I can’t put it into words,” Carter said. “Having a steady person in this program that people respect, he’s everything that you want as a coach.”

That stability carries added weight on a roster largely reconstructed during the offseason. While new faces fill much of the Hornets’ depth chart, Houston’s linebacker room remains a pocket of familiarity, with several of his longtime teammates returning to Sacramento.

Senior linebacker Alex Rocha arrived a year before him, while junior linebacker Fata Puloka joined him in the 2023 recruiting class. Senior linebacker Diego Davis joined the group in 2024, rounding out a core that has remained together through the program’s recent turnover.

“Even though we’ve been through a lot; personnel-wise and coaching, we always had each other to lean on and stick together with,” Houston said. “Those are some of my best friends, Diego, Alex, Fata. They’ve been my best friends for two years now. Having them to support when you come in with a new coach definitely helps a lot.”

The consistency Houston brings to the linebacker room carries over between the lines.

“He loves football, [he’s a] real physical player,” Carter said. “He plays hard. He is ‘100-100.’ That’s the type of kid you want, and that’s the type of kid I love coaching.”

After an offseason in which Houston was prepared to play his final years elsewhere, he’ll instead enter 2026 surrounded by familiar faces. His goals, for what could have been his first season elsewhere, are now tied entirely to the program he chose to return to.

“For me, I don’t really care what my stats are or stuff like that. I just want to make a bowl game,” Houston said. “Obviously, winning the MAC championship is the number one goal, but I think getting to be able to play in a bowl game would be huge, not only for this team but this entire community and university. All I really want to do is win. I just want to win.”

About the Contributor
Jack Dann, Sports Editor
(he/him) Jack Dann is a third-year journalism major from the Napa Valley in their third semester at The State Hornet. After gaining a following on social media covering the NBA and NFL, Jack joined The State Hornet and covered the women’s basketball and football beats in his first and second semesters, respectively. As a former college athlete and current scout, reporter and editor, Jack has experience at all levels of the field. He hopes to work in sports media and turn his passion into his career.
